title: GrowithAmazon
tagline: A full-service Amazon and marketplace growth platform — advertising, listing optimisation, catalogue and account management pulled into one professional digital ecosystem.
contribution: Translated a sprawling service catalogue into a navigable, conversion-oriented site architecture.
problem: Marketplace growth services are hard to sell because they're hard to explain. The offering spanned advertising, SEO, catalogue operations, vendor EDI and seller onboarding — and a brand arriving cold couldn't tell where it fitted or what to even ask for.
The previous structure mirrored the internal org chart rather than the customer's problem, so every enquiry started with a long clarifying conversation.
approach: Mapped every service into a hierarchy a seller would actually recognise — by the outcome they want, not by the team that delivers it.
Designed a component set (service cards, capability tiles, marketplace coverage, proof blocks) so new offerings drop into an existing pattern instead of needing bespoke design.
Kept exactly one primary action per screen, so the path to a conversation never competes with itself.
Built mobile-first and shared a single spacing and type scale across every template.
solution: A multi-section marketing platform with a structured services layer, marketplace coverage, case-study and update surfaces, and one consistent enquiry path running through every page.
Templates compose from the shared component set, so the visual system holds together as the service list grows.
impact: Services across eight marketplaces are discoverable from a single, coherent navigation model.
Non-technical team members publish new service pages without breaking the layout system.
The same component vocabulary now backs the wider product family, including the analytics dashboard.

title: Analytics Dashboard
tagline: A unified reporting surface for Amazon sellers and agencies — sales, inventory, returns and advertising pulled from a dozen connected platforms into one readable view.
contribution: Designed the KPI, trend and drill-down patterns that make multi-marketplace data legible at a glance.
problem: Sellers were reading their own business across a dozen disconnected consoles — Seller Central, Vendor Central, Amazon Advertising, Google Ads, Noon and more. Every question about performance began with an export and ended in a spreadsheet.
By the time a number was assembled by hand it was already stale, so decisions were being made on last week's picture.
approach: Started from the questions, not the data: what does an operator need to know in the first five seconds of opening this?
Built a strict hierarchy — headline KPIs, then trend, then breakdown, then row-level detail — so every module reads the same way and the eye learns the pattern once.
Chose chart types by the shape of the question: trend to line, comparison to bar, composition to stacked. Never decoration.
Designed the loading and empty states first, because a data product spends real time in both.
Used tabular figures and locale-aware formatting so columns of numbers stay aligned and scannable.
solution: A modular dashboard covering revenue analytics, inventory intelligence, returns analysis and advertising performance, with role-based workspaces separating multi-brand operators from agency accounts.
Reserved chart space and consistent number formatting keep the layout stable as data streams in, so nothing jumps while you're reading it.
impact: Performance questions that used to mean cross-referencing several consoles now resolve on one screen.
The module pattern absorbs new data sources without a redesign each time one is connected.
Reporting shifted from manual exports to a live, shareable surface.

title: WorkflowHub
tagline: An internal operations platform where tasks, tickets and daily account checks live in one workspace — with separate admin, manager and employee portals.
contribution: Built the board, task and role-based portal experience, including the Zoho Desk ticket sync surface.
problem: Marketplace operations ran on chat threads, spreadsheets and a separate helpdesk. Nobody could answer "who owns this and where is it" without asking three people.
Recurring per-account checks lived in individual habits rather than anywhere a manager could see, so coverage depended on who was at their desk.
approach: Modelled the real workflow first — task, owner, account, state — and designed around that instead of around a generic to-do list.
Gave each role only the surface it needs: admins configure, managers assign, employees execute.
Offered board, list and calendar views of the same data rather than forcing one mental model on everyone.
Brought support tickets into the same queue as internal work, so nothing lives in two systems at once.
solution: A workspace with kanban, list and calendar views, two-way Zoho Desk ticket sync, per-account daily checklists, file management with versioning, and dashboards for velocity and workload.
Authentication runs on JWT with httpOnly cookies, CSRF protection and encrypted sessions, with granular permissions behind each portal.
impact: Ownership and status are visible without a status meeting.
Support tickets and internal work sit in one queue instead of two systems.
Recurring account checks became a repeatable checklist rather than tribal knowledge.

title: CoTask
tagline: The public face of a technology and digital-growth agency — marketplace management, performance marketing and e-commerce development, all made legible to a first-time visitor.
contribution: Designed the service architecture and conversion-oriented layouts, and built the responsive frontend.
problem: The agency does a lot — seven marketplaces, five marketing channels, Shopify builds, vendor EDI account work. Presented as a flat list, that breadth read as unfocused rather than capable.
Credentials and partnerships were scattered as badges instead of building a case.
approach: Grouped services by the outcome a client wants, not by the internal team that delivers them.
Gave credentials and partnerships a dedicated proof layer where they reinforce each other.
Kept one low-friction consultation path, repeated at consistent intervals down the page.
Designed in Figma first, then built the same components in code so nothing drifted between file and production.
solution: A modern, conversion-oriented marketing site: outcome-grouped service tiles, marketplace coverage, a credentials strip, a blog surface, and a single recurring enquiry action.
Built responsive-first on a shared component set so new service pages inherit the system.
impact: A broad service range now reads as focused expertise rather than a menu.
Visitors can self-identify their need before ever speaking to sales.
New service pages drop into an existing pattern instead of needing bespoke design.

title: Paris Corner UAE
tagline: A premium Shopify storefront for a UAE fragrance house carrying nine sub-brands — where the product has to carry the page and the interface has to get out of its way.
contribution: Built the storefront end to end in Liquid — product presentation, collection browsing and the visual language that keeps a nine-brand catalogue feeling like one house.
problem: Nine sub-brands, hundreds of SKUs and heavy combo merchandising were all competing for the same attention. Shoppers browsing by scent and shoppers browsing by brand kept hitting dead ends.
Every merchandising change was a developer ticket, which meant the storefront moved slower than the marketing calendar.
approach: Let the photography lead: dark, quiet surfaces and thin gold rules instead of decorative chrome.
Made brand and scent both first-class browsing paths rather than nesting one inside the other.
Built the theme as composable Liquid sections, so merchandising can be rearranged without touching code.
Kept price, size and combo savings on one predictable line so comparison takes no effort.
solution: A restrained luxury storefront built entirely in Liquid on Shopify: a centred wordmark identity, editorial hero banners, brand and collection landing surfaces, and combo merchandising blocks.
The product card stays readable whether it holds a single bottle or a bundle, which is what lets one grid serve the whole catalogue.
impact: Nine sub-brands read as one house rather than nine competing storefronts.
Shoppers move brand → scent → bundle without leaving the browsing flow.
Merchandising changes ship through Shopify sections rather than developer tickets.
